newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Activists deported after East Timor meeting break-up.
newsitem.headline: Activists deported after East Timor meeting break-up.

text.p: Malaysia on Sunday deported nearly all the foreign activists detained after the break-up of a controversial conference on East Timor.
An immigration department spokesman at Kuala Lumpur international airport said all but 10 of the activists would have left on Sunday. The rest would leave on Monday.
The Kuala Lumpur conference was held ahead of Tuesday's anniversary of the 1991 killing by Indonesian troops of at least 50 demonstrators in East Timor's capital of Dili.
On Sunday, the police freed 26 Malaysian activists and the Singapore-based correspondent of the Australia Broadcasting Corporation, Catherine McGrath, on personal bonds.
Others, including Asiaweek's correspondent in Kuala Lumpur, Roger Mitton, were expected to be released the latest by Wednesday, lawyers for the activists said.

"What happened in the past two days has been an incredible shock to all of us. We are deeply concerned about the fate of our friends who have been deported," said Debbie Stothard, a spokesperson for the conference organisers.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Sunday described as unfortunate the detention of McGrath and activists by Malaysian police but said Canberra will not take action.
Howard said Australia would not take any action over the incident, noting the activists present at the conference knew it was prohibited and that they could be detained.
"I think it is an unfortunate incident but I am not going to take it beyond that," he told reporters.

Two of the deportees, Australian Andrew McNaughtan, 42, and Japanese Ihiro Kimura, 21, said the meeting on Saturday in a Kuala Lumpur hotel had just begun when members of a Malaysian youth group allied to Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's ruling coalition stormed in and broke it up.
"They ran amok, overturning chairs...and screaming...They were extremely threatening," McNaughtan told Reuters.
"I was frightened, very frightened...Really a spark at any moment (and) it could have turned into a bloodbath...It was very frightening because these people were quite irrational."
McNaughtan, convenor of the Australia East Timor Association in New South Wales, added: "It's pretty frightening when you are confronted with a couple of hundred people who are just crazy."
Kimura said the incident appeared to be "very well orchestrated".

"They came in, tore down all the banners," he said. "There may have been some looting, things were strewn across. We were in the middle of the floor trying to hold the circle. We were being yelled at from behind, from the front."
The Malaysian government denied backing the youths who broke up the meeting.
"They acted on their own. I was not notifed by them," Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told reporters.
Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, leader of the Mahathir's United Malays National Organisation's youth wing, confirmed that he ordered the conference disrupted to protect Malaysia's image.
The conference organisers and opposition leader Lim Kit Siang have accused the government of orchestrating the incident to scuttle the conference.

The foreign activists, including two Roman Catholic bishops -- Aloisuis Nobuo Somo of Nagoya, Japan and Hilton Deakin of Melbourne, Australia -- were detained by police after the meeting was broken up.
Supporters of the 80-year-old Japanese bishop said in Japan they were worried about his health, the Sankei Shimbun reported on Sunday.
"He told us before he left that it was quite likely he would be arrested," Father Toyohiko Hirata of the catholic diocese of Nagoya, told the Japanese daily.
"He said if anything happened he would contact us, but there's been no word until now. We are afraid for his health because of his old age," he told the newspaper.
